Thanks Marissa — this looks good. A few clarifying questions before the follow-up call:

1) Autoscaling: How fast can dedicated pools scale up for sudden traffic bursts? We sometimes see 5–8x increases for 3–7 minutes after batch jobs. Do you support pre-warmed burst capacity and what are the typical cold-standby times?

2) Concurrency & queues: Can you describe concurrency limits per model vs per-pool? We need to control max concurrent inferences per tenant to avoid noisy neighbor issues. Also, how do request queues behave when all workers are saturated (max queue length, retry/backoff policy)?

3) SDK/auth: For private deployments we will integrate the SDK into our backend services inside the VPC. How does auth work (short-lived tokens, mutual TLS, IAM integration)? Any sample code you can share for SDK initialization and routing by model variant?

4) Embeddings / Re-ranker: Do you recommend managing embeddings indexes on the same dedicated pool or a separate service? Our goal is sub-100ms P99 retrieval + rerank.

If you can share the sizing worksheet filled with your assumptions that would be super helpful for our infra team before Wed’s call.

Hi Carlos / Elaine — quick technical notes addressing your four questions (aiming to be concrete so your infra can validate). If helpful I can join Wed’s call and walk through the sizing worksheet step-by-step.

1) Autoscaling & burst capacity
- Dedicated pools support both scheduled scaling and reactive scaling based on token/s and concurrency metrics. For short spikes we recommend enabling "burst buffer" (pre-warmed GPUs) sized as a % of baseline. Typical config: baseline pool sized for 1.5x sustained load + 30% burst buffer for short-lived spikes.
- Cold-start for a new VM/GPU with model load varies by model size/format; for commonly used open models we optimize with precompiled kernels and checkpoint caching — typical spin-up is ~20–90s depending on model and backend (we can provide per-model profiles).
- For Finexa-like traffic (3–7min spikes 5–8x) we suggest a mix: small burst buffer and a short autoscale cooldown (60s) + fast prefetch for model weights. We’ll add exact numbers to the sizing sheet.

2) Concurrency limits & request queues
- Concurrency controls exist at two layers: per-worker (max concurrent inferences on a GPU instance) and per-tenant routing layer. You can set hard limits per-tenant to prevent noisy neighbor effects.
- When workers are saturated requests are queued at the routing layer. Queue behavior: FIFO with priority classes (low/normal/high). Configurable max queue length; beyond that requests are rejected with a 429 and retried by client with exponential backoff (default 200ms base).
- We also expose backpressure headers (X-Redwood-Queue-Depth, X-Redwood-Est-Wait) so your services can make smart retry decisions.

3) SDK & authentication
- Private deployments support short-lived JWTs minted by your identity provider (OIDC) or mTLS with customer-managed certs. We can integrate with your existing IAM (Okta/Azure AD) and KMS for key management.
- Example SDK initialization (pseudo-code):

  // Python SDK init with OIDC
  from redwood import RedwoodClient
  client = RedwoodClient(endpoint="https://private-api.finexa.redwood.local", auth=OIDC(token_provider))
  # route to dedicated pool / model variant
  resp = client.generate(model="finexa/rt-reranker:v2", input=prompt, route_policy={"pool":"dedicated-finexa-prod"})

- For routing you can pick by pool, model alias, latency SLA, or cost-tier. SDKs support explicit route hints and automatic policy-based routing.

4) Embeddings & re-ranker placement
- Best practice: Keep the embeddings index (ANN store) close to your query path. For sub-100ms P99 we often recommend a separate, lightweight vector-serving cluster colocated with the dedicated inference pool (same VPC/subnet) rather than hosting heavy ANN indexing on the GPU inference nodes. That avoids interference and allows independent scaling of vector search.
- We support local caching of top-k vectors on GPU nodes to accelerate rerank after retrieval. For retriever+rerank patterns we usually size the vector store for QPS and use a small GPU-backed rerank pool for final scoring.

Attachments: I updated the sizing sheet with baseline assumptions for Finexa (tokens per req, avg seq length, target P99) and included an architecture sketch showing where SDK, auth, routing, vector store and rerank pool sit. See attached files.

If you can confirm (a) peak sustained qps, (b) avg request tokens and (c) desired P99 latency we’ll finalize the recommended Dedicated pool config and autoscale knobs. I can also provide example nginx-ingress rules for routing into the private control plane if you want infra-friendly copy/paste.
